blocks.heading: What a hash actually does
text: Bitcoin, Git, and the login you used this morning all rest on the same function.
It is simpler than it looks, and stranger.

blocks.heading: A fixed-size fingerprint
text: A hash function takes input of **any** size and returns a number of **fixed** size. Four bytes or nine gigabytes, the answer is always 256 bits.

blocks.alt: Inputs of three different sizes all feeding into SHA-256 and producing one fixed-width output
blocks.caption: Information is destroyed on purpose. That is the point, not a flaw.

blocks.heading: Same in, same out
text: It is not random. The same input always gives the same digest, on any machine, forever.

blocks.heading: Change one letter
text: Those two inputs differ by a single character. The outputs have nothing in common.

blocks.alt: Two rows of bits; roughly half of the second row is highlighted as flipped
blocks.caption: Across the full digest, **131 of 256 bits** flipped - almost exactly half.

blocks.title: The avalanche property
text: Every input bit affects every output bit, about half the time. So the digest tells you _nothing_ about the input - not its length, not its content, not whether you were close.

blocks.heading: Why you cannot go backwards
text: There is no clever inverse. To reverse a digest you would have to guess inputs until one matches, and the space you are guessing in is this big:

blocks.caption: Roughly the number of atoms in the observable universe.

blocks.question: There are infinitely many possible inputs but only $2^{256}$ possible digests. So collisions must exist. Why is SHA-256 still considered safe?
answer: Because existing is not the same as findable. The birthday bound says you would need about $2^{128}$ attempts to stumble on any collision.
At a trillion hashes per second, that is far longer than the age of the universe. The collisions are real and permanently out of reach.

blocks.heading: Three properties, three attacks
text: A hash is only useful while all three hold. Each one has a name for how it breaks.

rows: Find _any_ input producing a given digest
Your document is the only one with its digest
Find a second input matching _your_ input
No two inputs share a digest
blocks.caption: MD5 and SHA-1 are broken in the third sense, which is why signatures moved on.

blocks.heading: This is what makes a chain

items.title: Each block stores the previous block's digest
Change any old transaction
items.text: That block's digest changes completely - the avalanche property guarantees it.

items.title: Now every later block is wrong
items.text: Each one points at a digest that no longer matches, all the way to the tip.

blocks.heading: The chain is the hash
text: There is no glue holding blocks together. The link **is** the digest, and tamper-evidence falls out of the maths for free.
Next: how a key proves _who_ wrote a transaction.
